solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Pay comedian less, essentially (5)

indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is its core, so take the middle of LESS

blocks.note: a wag is a joker
the middle two letters of LESS

annotation.surface: A penny-pinching promoter decides to pay the comic less than agreed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pay comedian less' reads as one instruction about a stingy booker, but 'Pay' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the weekly sum an employer hands over is both pay and wages.

entries.clue: With success, go over border of Lincolnshire town (10)

indicatorNotes.border of: a border is the edge, so take the outside letters of LINCOLNSHIRE
indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, one part sits over the next

blocks.note: w = with, as in w/
a hit is a success
to have a go = to have a stab
the first and last letters of LINCOLNSHIRE

annotation.surface: Someone crosses successfully into a town just across the Lincolnshire boundary.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts the town in Lincolnshire, but WHITSTABLE is a seaside town in Kent famous for oysters; Lincolnshire only supplies its two edge letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Whitstable is a town on the north Kent coast.

entries.clue: Chat cut short (3)

indicatorNotes.short: a word cut short loses its last letter

blocks.note: GASH (a cut) without its final H

annotation.surface: A conversation that ended abruptly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut short' looks like one phrase describing the chat; split it, and 'cut' is GASH, 'short' the instruction. To gas is British slang for chatting idly.
annotation.definitionFit: To gas is to chat at length about nothing much.

entries.clue: Alternate pronunciation of maritime proverb (6)

indicatorNotes.pronunciation of: we want how the phrase is said, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: sea = maritime, a saw is a proverb

annotation.surface: A sailors' saying that can be pronounced in more than one way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Alternate' pretends to be an adjective, as in an alternate pronunciation, but it is the verb: to swing back and forth.
annotation.definitionFit: To seesaw is to alternate between two states.

entries.clue: First-class meal and accommodation comprises good starting point (9)

indicatorNotes.comprises: the meal holds the first-class letter inside it

blocks.note: lunch is a meal
A = first-class, as in A1 or grade A; it goes inside LUNCH
a pad is a place to live

annotation.surface: A first-class hotel offering food and lodging is a fine base to set out from.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a travel review. A needs to sit between the L and the U of LUNCH, not stand at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A launchpad is where something starts off from, so a good starting point.

entries.clue: Services computers etc controlled by viruses? (9)

indicatorNotes.controlled by: held by, so the computers go inside the viruses

blocks.note: the lurgy is British slang for a minor bug going round
IT = information technology, computers and the like; it goes inside LURGIES

annotation.surface: A service department's machines have been taken over by computer viruses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Viruses' suggests computer malware, but here it means illnesses: the lurgy is British slang for whatever bug is going round the office.
annotation.definitionFit: Liturgies are forms of church service.

entries.clue: Doorkeepers ignoring heroin addicts (5)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: leave out the letter for heroin

blocks.note: ushers keep doors and show people in
H is slang for heroin; drop it from USHERS

annotation.surface: Bouncers turn a blind eye to junkies with heroin.
annotation.walkthrough: The drug theme runs through the surface, and 'heroin' is exactly what gets taken away.
annotation.definitionFit: Users are people who take drugs, addicts.

entries.clue: Those in debt supporting children, eating the last of tinned soups (8)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue, the debtors hold up the children from below
indicatorNotes.eating: the debtors take in a letter
indicatorNotes.the last of: take the final letter of TINNED

blocks.note: ch is the standard abbreviation for children
people who owe
the final letter of TINNED, inside OWERS

annotation.surface: Families in debt get by feeding their children tinned soup.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a picture of hard times, and the soups in it are the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Chowders are thick soups, often of fish or clams.

entries.clue: Pilots managed to arrest flyer over disruptive presence (11)

indicatorNotes.managed: the pilots are handled into a new order
indicatorNotes.to arrest: the rearranged pilots take the bird into custody
indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, the bird is turned upside down

blocks.note: PILOTS rearranged
EGRET, a heron-like bird, flipped; it goes inside POLIST

annotation.surface: Airline pilots arranged for a disruptive passenger to be arrested.
annotation.walkthrough: The aviation picture makes 'flyer' look like a passenger; it is a bird. 'Managed' is a less common anagram signal: the letters are handled into a new arrangement.
annotation.definitionFit: A poltergeist is a noisy spirit that throws things about, a disruptive presence.

entries.clue: Party drug hoax (4)

blocks.note: the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland
E = ecstasy

annotation.surface: A rumour about pills at a party that turns out to be fake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party drug' reads as one thing, ecstasy, but the party is a political one: the DUP is a Northern Irish party.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: fooling someone with a trick can be called either.

entries.clue: Enclose fashionable society magazine article missing introduction (9)

indicatorNotes.missing introduction: the article loses its first letter

blocks.note: in = in fashion
s = society
Heat is a British celebrity gossip magazine
THE without its T

annotation.surface: An editor slips a trendy society piece into a magazine without its opening paragraph.
annotation.walkthrough: Heat is a British weekly celebrity magazine. 'Enclose' is the verb: to insheathe is to put into a sheath.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind of enclosing: putting a sword or blade into its sheath.

entries.clue: Nil by mouth for one in bed? (5)

blocks.note: nil = nought, O
the multiplication sign, as in 2 by 4
lip = cheek, mouthing off

annotation.surface: A patient in a hospital bed is not allowed to eat or drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nil by mouth' is the hospital sign meaning no food or drink, so the bed looks like a hospital bed. It is a flower bed.
annotation.definitionFit: The oxlip is a primrose-like wild flower, one you might grow in a bed.

entries.clue: With regular instances of unrest, he and Islam tangled (6,7)

annotation.definition: With regular instances of unrest, he and Islam tangled

indicatorNotes.regular instances of: take every other letter of UNREST
indicatorNotes.tangled: the letters are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of UNREST
anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A man whose clashes with Islam repeatedly caused unrest.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: Salman Rushdie's novel The Satanic Verses led to a fatwa and riots, so he did tangle with Islam amid unrest.
annotation.definitionFit: Rushdie's run-ins with Islamic authorities after The Satanic Verses sparked repeated protests.

entries.clue: South of large uranium extraction facility, detect glowing (11)

indicatorNotes.South of: in a down clue, the detecting part sits below the rest

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing labels
U is the chemical symbol for uranium
a mine is where ore is extracted
to scent is to detect by smell

annotation.surface: Near a uranium mine, a detector picks up something glowing.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface leans on the cliché that radioactive things glow, which makes 'glowing' feel part of the story rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Luminescent means giving off light, glowing.

entries.clue: You are in a right mess with European Court icon (6,4)

indicatorNotes.in: the letters for 'you are' go inside the rest
indicatorNotes.with: the European letter is added on

blocks.note: used as it stands
rt is the abbreviation for right
to make a hash of = to make a mess of
text-speak for 'you are'; it goes inside HASH
E = European

annotation.surface: Someone is in legal trouble in front of the European Court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court: Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975. 'Mess' is a noun here, HASH, not an anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis champion, an icon of the court.

entries.clue: Charitable donations from key Liberal Welsh politician (4)

blocks.note: A is a musical key
L = Liberal
MS = Member of the Senedd, the Welsh parliament

annotation.surface: A leading Welsh Liberal hands out money to charity.
annotation.walkthrough: An MS is a Member of the Senedd, the Welsh parliament; 'key' is a musical key, not an important one.
annotation.definitionFit: Alms are money or food given to the poor.

entries.clue: Someone criticising lively drag parties heartlessly (10)

indicatorNotes.lively: the letters are jumped about into a new order
indicatorNotes.heartlessly: PARTIES loses its heart, the central T

blocks.note: anagram fodder, used as it stands
PARTIES without its middle letter T
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A killjoy is heartlessly running down some lively drag parties.
annotation.walkthrough: The heart comes out before the letters are rearranged: PARTIES has seven letters, so its heart is the single T.
annotation.definitionFit: A disparager is someone who belittles or criticises.

entries.clue: Withdrawing work put forward, puncturing the writer’s self-importance (9)

indicatorNotes.Withdrawing: drawing back, so the work runs backwards
indicatorNotes.puncturing: the proposal pierces the writer's word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: OP (opus, a work) turned round
the writer is the setter, so 'the writer's' = MY
to posit is to put forward an idea; it goes inside MY

annotation.surface: A writer withdraws a submitted piece, which takes his ego down a peg.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Puncturing self-importance' is a stock phrase, so the surface makes it one idea; here it is the placing instruction. In crosswords 'the writer' is the setter, giving MY.
annotation.definitionFit: Pomposity is an inflated sense of one's own importance.

entries.clue: Deviant is around person with outdated views (8)

indicatorNotes.Deviant: straying from the normal order of letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An old-fashioned bigot hangs around someone he considers deviant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deviant' looks like a noun, a person being judged, but it is an adjective telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A dinosaur is a person whose views have failed to move with the times.

entries.clue: Instil some reforms very slowly (10)

indicatorNotes.reforms: the letters are formed again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Advice to bring in change gradually.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reforms' looks like a noun, as in political reforms, but it is the verb telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Lentissimo is the musical direction for playing very slowly.

entries.clue: Periodically print the important part (4)

indicatorNotes.Periodically: at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of PRINTTHE

annotation.surface: An editor's instruction to print only the key section from time to time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' suggests a periodical, a magazine, in a clue about printing.
annotation.definitionFit: The pith of something is its essential, most important part.

entries.clue: Part of Ireland beginning to tax alcohol (6)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: take the first letter of TAX

blocks.note: County Clare, in the west of Ireland
the first letter of TAX

annotation.surface: An Irish region is starting to put a tax on drink.
annotation.walkthrough: County Clare is on Ireland's west coast. Claret is the British name for red Bordeaux wine.
annotation.definitionFit: Claret, red wine from Bordeaux, is an alcoholic drink.

entries.clue: Eventually, King, Queen and others turned on very old emperor (6,2,5)

indicatorNotes.turned: the queen and others run backwards
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one part comes after the other

blocks.note: so = very, as in so good
o = old
the Roman emperor
R = rex, king
R (regina) + ET AL (and others), turned round

annotation.surface: In time, the royal family and courtiers rose against an ancient emperor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as 'attacked', but it splits: 'turned' reverses the queen and others, 'on' puts them after the emperor. Rex and regina both give R.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for an unspecified future moment, a plain equivalent of the single adverb.

entries.clue: Resin from tree, one packed with energy (5)

indicatorNotes.packed with: the tree is filled with the energy letter

blocks.note: the elm tree
E = energy, as in E = mc²; it goes inside ELM
the Roman numeral for one

annotation.surface: Resin comes from a tree, one full of vitality.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes resin come from a tree, which is true, so 'from' works as a link rather than a signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Elemi is a fragrant resin from tropical trees, used in varnishes and incense.

entries.clue: Fleece coats sent north (4)

indicatorNotes.sent north: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

blocks.note: macs, short for mackintoshes, are raincoats

annotation.surface: Fleece jackets and coats are being shipped up north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fleece' pretends to be a garment beside the coats; it is the verb, to swindle. A mac is a British word for a raincoat.
annotation.definitionFit: Fleece in its slang sense of swindling someone out of money, as a shearer strips a sheep.
annotation.definitionNote: Fleece is a verb here and SCAM is used as a verb too.

entries.clue: Section of church elated Hindu disciple (5)

indicatorNotes.Section of: the answer is a piece cut from the words that follow

blocks.note: churCH ELAted

annotation.surface: Part of a church congregation is delighted by a Hindu follower.
annotation.walkthrough: The religious surface blends church and Hindu so the definition feels like part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: A chela is a pupil or disciple of a guru in Hinduism.

entries.clue: Those leaving the country record label before awards (9)

indicatorNotes.before: 'before' in the sense of ahead of in order, so the label is written ahead of the awards

blocks.note: EMI is a British record company
grants = awards of money

annotation.surface: Musicians quitting the country sign with a record label before award season.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Awards' suggests music prizes in a record-industry surface, but it means grants of money.
annotation.definitionFit: Emigrants are people leaving their country to settle abroad.

entries.clue: Clear of all charges, X is on the rise (3)

indicatorNotes.on the rise: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten

annotation.surface: A price that includes nothing extra, while inflation keeps climbing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear of all charges' sounds like an acquittal in court; it means a sum after deductions.
annotation.definitionFit: A net amount is what remains after all charges and deductions.

entries.clue: Couple briefly trying swimming for pregnant women (9)

indicatorNotes.briefly: cut the word short, dropping its last letter
indicatorNotes.swimming: the letters move about into a new order

blocks.note: to mate is to couple
TRYING without its G, rearranged

annotation.surface: A pair quickly try out swimming classes designed for expectant mothers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks as if it trims 'Couple', but it works on 'trying'. Maternity is used as an adjective, as in maternity wear, which fits 'for pregnant women'.
annotation.definitionFit: Maternity clothes or wards are ones intended for pregnant women.
annotation.definitionNote: MATERNITY is used attributively (maternity wear), matching the phrase 'for pregnant women'.

entries.clue: Perhaps Mr Levy has left for hotel (5)

indicatorNotes.has left for hotel: swap H (hotel) out and L (left) in

blocks.note: a tithe is a levy of a tenth
L = left replaces H = hotel (NATO alphabet)

annotation.surface: A man named Levy has checked out of his hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mr Levy' reads as a person's name; split it, and 'Perhaps Mr' is the definition while Levy is a tax.
annotation.definitionFit: Mr is an example of a title, hence 'perhaps'.
